questions.q: In the capstone's two tool schemas, why does issue_refund's description explicitly state that it requires human approval, if the description itself doesn't enforce that?
options: It has no real purpose and is purely decorative
It's good practice so the model's own explanations of its plan reflect reality, even though the actual enforcement happens in your application code, not the description text
The Claude API requires this exact phrase in every tool description
It replaces the need for any code-level checkpoint
questions.explain: The description helps the model's own behavior (how it explains what it's about to do) match reality, but the lesson is explicit that your code — not the description — is what actually enforces the checkpoint.

questions.q: How does the capstone's handle_tool_use code decide whether a tool call needs to go through the approval path?
options: Every tool call, without exception, goes through approval
It checks the tool name on each tool_use block — only issue_refund is routed to queue_for_approval, while get_order executes immediately
It randomly selects which calls require approval
It approves calls automatically after a fixed delay regardless of tool name
questions.explain: The code explicitly branches on block.name, sending only issue_refund through the approval-hold path and letting get_order run immediately — a direct application of Lesson 18's rule of thumb.

questions.q: In the full round trip this lesson traces, what happens immediately after Claude calls issue_refund?
options: The tool executes immediately with no delay
The API returns stop_reason: tool_use, and your code recognizes this tool needs approval, persists the pending request, and stops the loop rather than executing right away
The conversation ends permanently
Claude automatically cancels the refund request
questions.explain: Because issue_refund is a gated tool, the loop stops at the tool_use block and the request is queued for human review, rather than being executed immediately like get_order.

questions.q: Which safety-layer items does this lesson's build explicitly leave out on purpose, to be added in Lesson 30?
options: The tool schemas themselves, which aren't defined until Lesson 30
Audit logging, stopping conditions, a cost budget, and scoped credentials
The approval checkpoint itself, which is deferred to Lesson 30
The get_order tool, which doesn't exist until Lesson 30
questions.explain: This lesson focuses on proving the approval mechanism works end to end; audit logging, stopping conditions, budgets, and credential scoping are explicitly deferred to Lesson 30's build on the same foundation.

questions.q: If the human reviewer rejects the issue_refund request in the round trip, how should the resulting tool_result differ from the approved case, per Lesson 19's format this lesson reuses?
options: It should be identical to the approved case, since the tool still technically ran
No tool_result should be sent at all if the request is rejected
It should use the same tool_use_id, but set is_error: true with an explanation in content, and the real refund tool should never actually execute
The tool_use_id should be changed to indicate a new, unrelated request
questions.explain: A rejection reuses the same tool_use_id in a tool_result block, sets is_error: true, and explains the decision in content — the real refund never executes, exactly as Lesson 19 established.
